silo_relevance: This paper is highly relevant to risk_management because it focuses on quantum methods for VaR/CVaR estimation, tail-risk computation, and credit-portfolio risk modeling. Its main value for this silo is the comparison of quantum Monte Carlo, comparator/binary-search VaR estimation, and the practical bottlenecks that affect whether these methods can improve risk measurement workflows.

key_points.point: The paper directly frames risk management as estimating VaR/CVaR and tail losses, which is the core target of the silo.
key_points.silo_note: This is the most direct match to risk_management because the silo is specifically about VaR, CVaR, stress testing, and tail-risk estimation.

key_points.point: Quantum Monte Carlo is presented as the main quantum route for risk estimation, with a theoretical precision scaling improvement and a VaR strategy based on comparator plus binary search.
key_points.silo_note: These are the central algorithmic ideas for faster risk metric estimation, especially for repeated VaR queries.

key_points.point: The paper emphasizes that risk analysis is harder than pricing because tail estimation is more demanding than expectation estimation.
key_points.silo_note: For risk_management, this matters because the hardest part is not pricing but accurately resolving rare-loss tails that drive VaR/CVaR.

key_points.point: Classical risk workflows are reviewed alongside credit-portfolio dimensionality reduction methods such as PCA and factor models, which are the baseline that quantum methods aim to improve.
key_points.silo_note: This is important for credit risk and portfolio risk modeling, where high-dimensional dependence structures make classical estimation expensive.

key_points.point: The paper is cautious that quantum risk speedups depend on hard-to-realize loading/oracle assumptions, and that distribution loading can dominate runtime.
key_points.silo_note: For risk_management, this limits near-term deployability because VaR/CVaR gains may disappear if market or credit-loss distributions are expensive to encode.

_r1_caveat: L3 #3 is real but narrow: the PDE bullet drops the survey's own limitations (non-Hermitian H_BS requiring auxiliary qubit + post-selection; unassessed variational scaling). The two themes this paper feeds (DT-RM-004 loading bottleneck, DT-RM-010 quadratic-speedup contingent on oracle/loading) are accurately supported; do not cite this memo for any PDE-route claim without revising the bullet.
